issues.legal_issue: A uniform tax on different crop-yielding plantations does not violate equality merely because the plantations differ in yield or profitability when the tax scheme uses measures intended to equalize the burden and hostile unequal treatment is not established.
material_facts: The tax applied to land used for specified plantations, and only land on which crops had begun to yield was included.

For several plantation types, the taxable extent was calculated by converting the number of yielding plants or trees into an area; for tea and cardamom, the taxable extent was the land on which the plants were grown and had begun to yield crops.
The petitioners relied on differing yields and profits among tea estates and argued that the uniform rate treated unequal plantations alike.
The Court found that the legislature had attempted to equalize the tax burden across plantation types and that the evidence did not establish hostile or unequal treatment among plantations.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the uniform tax was not shown to be discriminatory and rejected the equality challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to taxation, but legislatures have wide latitude to select taxable subjects, methods, and rates. A person challenging a tax bears a heavy burden to establish hostile unequal treatment, not merely possible inequality. Differences in treatment must be reasonably explained by the legislation’s object, and where different subjects are treated equally there must be a reasonable basis for equalizing their differences. The Court applied Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, East Indian Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income Tax Officer; it distinguished Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Nalla Raja Reddy, New Manek Chowk Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, and State of Kerala v. Haji K. Kutty Naha.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax: A person challenges a tax measure on constitutional equality grounds.
predicates.tax_limited_to_yielding_plantations: The taxing authority imposes the tax only on land used for specified crops that have begun to yield.
predicates.plantation_extent_measured_to_equalize_b: The taxing authority uses measures such as yielding-plant counts or crop-yielding land area to compare plantation extents for taxation.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_establish_hostile_une: The person challenging the tax does not conclusively establish that similarly situated taxpayers were treated unequally or that unequal treatment was hostile.

issues.definition: When a constitutional tax challenge concerns a tax limited to yielding plantations, the tax is not invalid for discrimination if its measurement is intended to equalize burdens or the challenger fails to establish hostile unequal treatment.

issues.legal_issue: The State legislature’s competence to impose land tax was no longer open to dispute after the state land-tax enactment received constitutional protection.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the legislature’s competence to impose a tax on land.
The state land-tax enactment had been included in the Ninth Schedule and received the protection of Article 31-B.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the legislature’s competence to impose land tax was no longer open to dispute and rejected that challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-B protects enactments included in the Ninth Schedule from specified constitutional challenges. The Court relied on the inclusion of the state land-tax enactment in that Schedule and concluded that the legislature’s competence to impose land tax was no longer open to dispute.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_land_t: A person challenges whether a state legislature has competence to impose a tax on land.
predicates.state_land_tax_enactment_has_constitutio: The state land-tax enactment has been included in a constitutionally protected schedule.

issues.definition: When a challenge to state legislative competence concerns land taxation and the state land-tax enactment has constitutional protection, the competence to impose land tax is not open to challenge.
